title: Building Software That Survives • Michael Nygard & Charles Humble

segments.text: [music]
Welcome to the GoTo Podcast. Each
episode covers the brightest and boldest
ideas from the world's leading experts
in software [music] development. Tune in
for practical lessons, compelling
theories, and plenty of inspiration.
[music]
Go to gathers the brightest minds in the
software community to help developers
tackle projects today, [music] plan for
tomorrow, and create a better future.
Stay up tod date with the latest in
[music] tech through GOTO's toprated
events held online and in person in
cities like Amsterdam, London, [music]
Copenhagen, and Chicago and by
subscribing to the GoTo conferences
YouTube channel [music] where you can
find thousands more highquality dev
talks. Learn more at gotopia.te.
[music]
Hello and welcome to this episode of
Goto Unscripted. I'm Charles Humble. I'm
a freelance techie, editor, author, and
consultant. And this is part of a series
of podcasts that I'm doing for GoTo
talking to software engineering leaders.
Today we're joined by Michael Nygard.
Michael is currently general manager of
the architecture enablement group at New
Bank, which is a very interesting and
successful financial services company.
>> [snorts]
>> He's, a, much, sought-after, conference
speaker and has written and co-authored
several books including 97 things every
software architect should know and the
bestseller release it which is a book
about building software that survives
the real world and was a huge influence
on my own career. I'm thrilled to have
you on Michael welcome to the show.
>> Hi, Charles,, I'm, delighted, to, be, here.
>> Thank, you., So, I've, sort, of, described
your career to some extent but can you
maybe talk about it from your
perspective? What is it that you would
say that you do in a general sense?
Yeah, that's always a surprisingly hard
question to ask. In fact, I I I don't
expect an existential crisis at the
passport control line. But when they ask
me what I do, I sort of say, well, I
used to be a programmer.
And and it's true. That's where I began.
You know, I was a programmer and then an
architect. And for about the last 10
years, I've been in this sort of fuzzy
space that we call tech leadership or
technology leadership, which is, you
know, applying what I understand about
systems and people and organizations and
architecture to try to help companies
succeed in their objectives. And it is a
little bit nebulous and a little bit
vague around the edges. So when somebody
asks what do I do, I usually just say
I'm in technology now.
>> Yes., Yes,, I, I, I, can, relate., So, I,, as, I
said in the intro, I think I came across
you, as I suspect many of us did
through release it originally, through
that book, which was is such an
important work, I think. So can you talk
a bit about that book? How did it come
into being?
>> Yeah., First, of, all,, I'm, I'm, glad, that
you found it useful. I never get tired
of hearing that people found it valuable
and and influential.
It came about through kind of a chaotic
set of circumstances in my life. a
consulting company that I had founded
with or co-founded with great timing at
the beginning of 2001. We had gone along
for a while but decided that it
ultimately wasn't working. And I was
casting about looking for some kind of
contract I could take, put in just, you
know, 40 hours a week, go home, recover
from the the stresses of that consulting
company. And what I ended up doing was
getting a contract that turned into 60
70, 80 hour weeks for the next two
years.
So it was it was not exactly the
relaxing venture I'd hoped for, but it
was a step in a different direction.
Instead of being a developer, I was in
this role called application
administrator, which meant I didn't have
root privileges, but I was there to
write all the configs for the web
servers and the app servers and and help
get this commerce site up and running.
And so it was essentially an operational
role at first mainly focused on QA and
then
trying to move into production. I
started asking a lot of annoying
questions like how are we going to
manage all these configurations for
production because we've got a whole
bunch of machines and different
instances. And it turns out when you ask
too many annoying questions that nobody
has answers to, eventually you get
tasked with solving those. And so I I
designed and built the production
infrastructure for that system that we
were launching. And then I once it
launched I was there with the care and
feeding and the 3:00 a.m. crashes and
the sudden you know operational outages.
But because I had come from development
I was able to do things like look at the
stack traces from the application server
and go tell the developers this is
exactly where all of your threads are
getting hung up and it's why your pages
are not showing up and the the app
server was unresponsive. And it would be
something like you know get a connection
from a connection pool with no timeout.
So just wait infinitely. and then
something else would be holding a
connection and throw an exception and
bust out of its stack and never release
the connection and you have a deadlock.
So I was in that space where I was a
developer in operations quite a few
years before we started talking about
DevOps. So I was able to bridge these
two worlds that had had drifted apart
during the early web ops days and it was
a great education for me because I saw
that in ops the standard solution is you
know have you tried turning it off and
back on again? Mhm.
>> And, most, of, the, time, that, worked,, but, it
was very disruptive and
it it it just sort of got under my skin
as an engineer that we were creating
such awful software that had to be
restarted several times a day just to
keep up and running.
>> And, so, that, was, sort, of, the, genesis, of
it. I I started looking at the problems
and I saw that the problems came in
types or classes. And that was actually
an encouraging discovery because if
there are types of problems then maybe
there are categorical solutions and I
started looking for those and that
that's what became the book.
>> Right., Yes., Yeah., It's, there, was, such, an
interesting time that because I think
that whole business of how as you say
kind of operations and development sort
of drifted into these two very separate
camps and it was never really going to
work. And I think lots of us in
different ways were kind of
independently trying to figure out ways
of of bringing them back together. And
that was sort of what fed into the
DevOps movement. It didn't kind of
appear in isolation. But I think it's so
interesting that that was kind of
paralleled with your experience and
prompting the book as well. I think
that's fascinating. [snorts] You're
involved with this remarkable technology
transformation project at Sabre, which
is an interesting company in its own
right. So can you tell us a bit about
what Saber does and maybe a bit about
the underlying system and architecture
there?
>> Sure., So, I, have, sometimes, referred, to
Saber as the first software as a service
company.
>> Mhm.
>> Because, back, when, Saber, got, started,, it
was the first electronic booking system
and the first one to be offered to
multiple airlines. So it was built
within American Airlines as a mainframe
system. The main frame was actually
named Saber and it allowed travel agents
to reserve seats on on planes. Saber
started offering that to you know
multiple airlines and connecting agents
to those airlines and running the
passenger support system. So it all
began on mainframes and when I joined
still the majority of revenue eventually
went through the main frames in one way
or another. Over the years, there had
been successive attempts to, you know
take things off of the mainframe and
build different types of systems, some
monoliths, some mega serviceservices
some microservices later on. But there
was this environment of 50 years of
accumulated technical debt, some data
centers that Saber had been occupying
since the 1970s
and really a a a technology portfolio
that no human being could fully
understand.
In in that realm, I came in with the the
task of modernizing development
practices, testing practices, moving to
continuous delivery and moving to the
cloud. At first, we had a multi cloud
strategy. Then we eventually settled on
Google Cloud as the the single target
and had the mission to, you know, get
everything to Google Cloud except the
main frames in a a pretty short period
of time.
It was fascinating because we had
initially thought the challenge would be
the cloud portion of it, but what we
actually discovered was that there had
been this extended period of what I
think was underfunding
in keeping the technology current. So
that we had applications running on
every version of Windows, every version
of of Linux you could think of. When I
joined, there was some HPUX, some
Solaris, there was probably a Vax off in
a corner someplace. And so really the
the biggest challenge was the
modernization of dev practices, getting
people just doing automated builds
continuous integration, and automated
testing. Like that was the first huge
hurdle. And I think we underestimated
the challenge of that when we started.
>> [snorts]
>> And, we, used, to, because, so, the, heart, of
Saber at one point was something called
TPF if I remember rightly which was a
sort of very unusual realtime operating
system. So it's very different from ZOS
and things like that. Was that still
there when you were working there? Was
that still kind of a core part of the
the the architecture?
>> TPF, was, still, there, when, I, joined, and, it
was still there when I left although the
the amount being done on it had changed
throughout that time. So yes, TPF is is
sort of an evolutionary branch that most
of the world never pursued. A real-time
[snorts] operating system on a
mainframe,
highly interrupt driven, very different
architecture than anything else you've
seen, but it delivers extremely high
volume throughput with very predictable
latency.
The downside is if it can't serve the
request within the latency windows, it
just refuses to accept it. quite
different than the kind of Unix model
where it's like you know throw as many
connections as you like I'll queue them
up I'll have enough threads I'll get
around to it sometime
>> right, yes
>> TPF, has, a, lot, of, attractive, attributes
and the the throughput at the cost is
it's actually pretty good
there just aren't a lot of people who
know how to do it anymore and you really
have just one vendor for your hardware
your operating system operations. So
it's it's the ultimate in lock in
>> right?, Yeah., Yeah., It's, fascinating., And
[snorts] as part of the sort of updating
the stuff, so you you said that you've
got a lot of what's effectively sort of
underinvested
legacy systems on endless different
operating systems and so on. So, you're
doing you're updating things, you're
paying down technical debt or however
you want to express that and you're
migrating to the cloud. Are you also
doing sort of structural things within
the organization at the same time? So
are you are you kind of changing the the
nature of the way the the tech
organization is working as you're as
you're doing the modernization process?
>> That, was, definitely, happening., It, it, was
sort of one step above my pay grade. So
my boss was part of a couple of big
reorganizations. one moving us to a
functional structure where it had been
the case that there were multiple
business units that each had their own
development and then there was the sort
of corporate portion that was meant to
be common platforms and common
technology and we moved to a a single
engineering org shortly after I joined.
This was one of the successive waves of
kind of centralization and
decentralization that had happened there
which many people you know regarded with
some skepticism and a little cynicism
about you know well I guess the pendulum
is swinging the other way now but uh
that was one of the big organizational
changes on the business side of things.
The two separate business units were
unified. One was aimed at serving the
the airlines. The other was aimed at
serving travel agencies and those were
brought together as well as a single
product organization.
>> So, just, to, to, clarify, that, you're, you're
essentially moving from a sort of
centralized command and control type
structure to something that is more of
an autonomous more of a liberated
structure. Is that is that what was kind
of going on at the same time?
Well,
it's it's interesting when we talk about
centralization versus autonomy because I
think people often view it as as a
single spectrum and you're either going
in one direction or you're going in the
other direction.
But what I have come to believe is that
you have to talk about centralization
versus autonomy with respect to certain
activities that you do. what are the
things that you can do independently and
what are the things that you have to go
through the decentralized authority for.
>> So, a, classic, example, finance, is
typically not autonomous. You have a
certain leeway to make spending
decisions within your organization but
you normally can't commit millions of
dollars of the company's capital without
getting some approval from a central
authority. So you have you know autonomy
within within limits but you also have
centralization for some governance and
control. So there you have a type of
activity and a degree of autonomy to
talk about. So what we went through at
Saber was creating a degree of autonomy
around deployment and build processes
that had been fully centralized in an
operations group that was being some of
it was being devolved to the the
individual teams but not all of it
because they couldn't just decide to go
hire their own data center and move a
bunch of hardware into it. they couldn't
decide to opt out of security monitoring
tools and that sort of thing. So
increasing autonomy in some dimensions
but actually increasing centralization
in other dimensions simultaneously.
>> That's, such, an, interesting, insight., I
think it's a really it's a really good
point and one that gets missed so often.
How does that compare with what you have
at New Bank where you are now? So, New
Bank really strongly endorses autonomy
maybe more than is practicable at a uh a
scaled up startup, but it is again it's
autonomy in certain activities supported
by structures. I know I'll give you some
examples. We have a few hundred squads
that are working on a few thousand
microservices.
Each squad is on their own pace for when
they build features, when they do
deployments, you know, it's all it's all
git driven operations now. So when they
merge a pull request, a deployment
happens and that's entirely on their
schedule,
but it works at scale because we have
the supporting structures that allow
them to do that. So we have, you know, a
build pipeline that everything goes
through. We have an architecture that
expresses a lot of the services
attributes as data and then we have
tooling that was built in the early days
that helps examine that data and make
sure that the service is safe to deploy.
And so you know we are enabling autonomy
in those activities like writing code
merging code, deploying code by creating
the structures that make it safe to do
that at scale.
>> That's, really, interesting., There's
something that I have come across and
I've kind of come to think of it as kind
of like a day two problem. So you've
you've had some sort of organizational
transformation and you've given people
more autonomy and then suddenly you have
to figure out how you keep the company
moving towards a common goal or a common
objective.
And
I think it's one of those things that
kind of often gets overlooked. There are
tools for that that are quite effective
tools, but if you haven't really thought
about how you're going to do it when you
can end up in a situation where the
organization is kind of pulling in all
sorts of different directions. I was
curious if you sort of had any thoughts
on that or any any reflections on on
tools or approaches that you've seen
work.
>> Sure., First, though,, I, have, to, I, have, to
say one of our slogans is it's always
day one. So, I'm officially not allowed
to talk about day two and day two
problems.
At New Bank, we started as a single
product company in one geography. We
were offering a mass market credit card
in Brazil.
>> Mhm.
>> And, since, then,, we, have, added, more
products in investments, loans, deposit
accounts,
and we're in multiple countries. We're
in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia.
We've also scaled up. We had a period of
hyperrowth in our customer base and in
our organization.
So alignment is a constant challenge.
It's something that we spend a lot of
effort on. We used OKRs from an early
stage. And so that's, you know, a tool
that's commonly recognized as helping to
drive alignment.
>> Mhm.
>> I'll, say, it, helps., OKRs, by, themselves
are not sufficient because you'll often
have multiple, you know, top level teams
directly facing the market that each
have their OKRs. You know, where we are
in Brazil is very different than where
we are in Colombia. And therefore, the
things we need to do in Brazil, very
different than the things we need to do
in Colombia. And then, of course, that
means that we have, you know, market
forces pulling us in different
directions at the very beginning. And
you percolate that through a layer of
global products and then global
platforms. And you know you often have
multiple OKRs that are asking for
different things from the same people.
So OKRs are part of it. We are also
working on high trust methods something
it's called high performing teams
attempting to get most of the leadership
speaking a common language about active
communication conflict surfacing
conflict resolution. This is all very
squishy stuff to most engineers, but you
can see the results when you look at a
management team that even if they're not
all pulling in the same direction, they
have common tools for acknowledging
that, surfacing it, and and working out
the the differences.
Even so, we put a lot of effort into
alignment. And one of the things I'm
doing is constantly looking for
situations where architectural
boundaries would enable more autonomy
and therefore require less effort
expended on alignment. Now, that's a
little bit of a complicated causal
chain, but I'll give an example or an
analogy like this.
Suppose you are you have green space
behind your house and four other
families also open up into that same
green space and you want to plant a
garden. Well, you probably need to talk
to your neighbors because you're
modifying some shared space. You're
taking use of it for your own purposes.
You have to negotiate like I'll give you
some cabbage or or whatever or I'll give
you more zucchini than you would ever
want.
Whereas if if you actually had fences
and you knew the boundaries of what was
yours, you could do what you needed to
do in that space with less effort spent
on negotiation and working out the
boundaries and parameters. And so
there's a sense in which you know
knowing the boundaries of where you can
operate freely increases your autonomy
within that area even though you do have
boundaries. So architecturally speaking
we talk a lot about boundaries. We look
at coupling inside and across those
boundaries and we try to find good
boundaries that, you know, make for good
fences and make for good neighbors.
>> That's, yeah,, that's, very, interesting.
That almost gets us into sort of
Conway's law territory, which we haven't
really touched on, but so Conway's law
is that, you know, I'll just quote it
because it's one of those things that
gets banded around. says it's
organizations which design systems in
the broadest sense are constrained to
produce designs which are copies of the
communication structures of these
organizations. And I think it's one of
those things that gets branded around a
lot but I think there's some really
quite interesting quite subtle aspects
to it that maybe get missed. I don't
know if you want to kind of reflect on
that a bit.
>> Uh, I, would, love, to., I, think, it's, super
important. In fact, Conway's law is is
very well understood by the leadership
at New Bank and was something that we
were trying to teach to the leadership
at Saber.
One of the the most interesting aspects
about Conway's law is is that people
often leave out the word communications
when talking about the structure. And so
they talk about, you know, the software
will mirror the structure of the
organization. That's not what he said.
It will mirror the communication
structure. So, what I've often seen is
companies reorganize
with an intent to have things operate
differently,
create a better cohesion among these
groups that you're bringing together
create a boundary between the groups
that you're separating.
But if you only change the formal
structure and you don't also change the
communication structure, then the the
change will not produce the effects you
expect under Conway's law.
There's a great book called Team
Topologies that had a section in it that
blew my mind and was clearly evidently
true once once you assimilated
but it it stated that communication is
not an absolute good. If you're
observing excess communication
between platform users and a platform
team, it might indicate that your
platform is inadequate or that the APIs
are not welld designigned or that you've
you've missed an abstraction. And so
that that notion of using a surplus of
communication where it doesn't need to
be as a a smoke detector was kind of a
wild idea, but it absolutely fits along
with Conway's law that if you expect
there to be an interface in the software
and you're not observing an interface in
the communication structure, you you
won't get what you want from the
software.
>> Yeah,, 100%., I, think, there's, a, sort, of
related thing that I've seen. I've only
seen it once, but it was and it was very
early on in my career when I was very
genius. I wasn't really involved in it
but it was a a large investment bank and
they were having all sorts of problems
and they bought in McKenzie. They
brought in, you know, a large consulting
firm and the McKenzie people recommended
this new very complex, very hierarchical
structure that was extremely difficult
to implement. [snorts] But they also, as
far as I could work out, paid very
little attention to how things were
actually being done. And what we ended
up with was the kind of the official
organization chart and then this sort of
unofficial shadow chart that, you know
we talk about shadow it a lot, but this
was like a whole shadow organization
where the actual structure didn't look a
lot like the official structure.
Is that something you you've seen? You
were nodding. [laughter]
>> Absolutely., and, and, especially, if, you
have a place where there are people with
high tenure who have known each other
for, you know, decades, they know each
other's kids and so on, you'll never
stop them from talking to each other.
And sometimes the most effective way to
get things done is to utilize that
network. But
>> yes,
>> you, risk, falling, into, this, worst, of, both
worlds situation where you have formal
systems and formal processes and you
know, Jira tickets for everything and
service now in place. you have a
procurement process and a procurement
system, but nothing actually happens
until you get one of the, you know
tenureworked people to poke somebody
else. And so like you you can eventually
access the speed of that high trust
network, but you've also got the weight
of the bureaucracy of the formal
processes that just don't work. or you
have to exercise the informal network
first and then the formal process is
just like you know the the paperwork
that you do after all the decisions are
already made. So if you want to use the
network style and and have that you know
high-speed lateral high trust
communication that's great. If you want
to have the formal processes that's
great but one or the other ought to work
[laughter] without needing to to engage
both of them every time.
>> Yeah., Yeah,, I, think, there's, something
it's, related, or, at least, it's, related, to
my my brain which is to do with tooling
and where we have like workflow
automation and admin tooling that itself
kind of ends up encoding a structure and
then you go and change the structure but
you don't change the tooling. And so
you've now got this sort of weird
disconnect between how the workflow
automation works and how the
organization is supposed to work. Again
is that a thing you've seen?
>> Yes., And, I've, seen, an, entire, industry
grow up around trying to to solve that
by enabling the users of the processes
to do their own automation in one way or
another. You know, it used to be that
the most effective departments were the
ones that had, you know, the the couple
of people who knew how to run Microsoft
Access and Visual Basic to serve the
immediate needs of that department
without getting tied up in, you know, it
scheduling.
These days, we tend to refer to RPA
because giving something a three-letter
acronym makes it, you know, less
distasteful uh as as a a band-aid over
tools that are always, you know, two
reorgs behind.
Automation and reaction is a classic
problem and it
you can reduce but not eliminate the lag
on tooling behind the organization by
putting more of that automation directly
in the hands of the users. And I think
what we're going to see over the next
year or two is a lot of adoption of
Agentic AI as the latest incarnation of
solving the tools problem. uh so that I
can just have the AI go and figure out
how to get my needs met in the current
organizational structure.
>> What's, your, take, on, that, as, an, approach?
Do you think that's something that's
likely to help? Something that's likely
to work just more noise?
I I think it's likely to help the users
of corporate processes particularly. You
know, we're seeing a lot of interest in
MCP and that as a way of making systems
more usable by the agents. I think
there's a risk that we're pouring
concrete on the problem instead of
solving the problem. you know, meaning
we may lose adaptability in the lower
layer and and just have this, you know
layer of agents in the middle trying to
to keep up. I'm not entirely sure how
that's going to play out in practice.
>> Yes., Yes., I, I, I, too, am, not, sure., I, think
I think I I have certainly seen an awful
lot of attempts of of using tooling to
paper over a problem that's really an
organizational problem. And really the
only way to fix an organizational
problem is to fix the organizational
problem. I think but it may be that it
can that it can help in some way.
>> Maybe, I, will, say, you, know, I've, been, in
this industry for a while now and I've
seen 4GL's
VB and and GUI builders. I've seen
screen scrapers and RPA. I've seen
agents. I've seen low code platforms.
Like all of these are attempts to put
some control directly in the hands of
the end users and they're, you know
they're all beneficial
but they're always sort of on the
periphery of what, you know, the real IT
inside the company is doing and that
makes it hard for them to stay current
and continue to have traction.
>> Yes., And, I, think, often
you know people who are not IT people
don't see it as their job to build
automation tools or you know as it might
be database querying tools or or
whatever it is. And so I think it's
quite a you know quite a difficult thing
if I'm I don't know an HR manager or
something and you say you know we've got
this wonderful new way of solving your
problem. It's like well I don't that's
not my job. My job is managing people.
[laughter]
So yeah, I just think it's tricky.
>> Yeah,, indeed., And, the, people, in, it, don't
don't necessarily see it as their job to
sort of do the last mile of, you know
knitting together four different
corporate systems so that the end user
isn't swiveing between them or [snorts]
you know it's it's very common if you go
and watch people engaging with the sort
of corporate side of the world. I'm not
talking about software development for
for serving customers but the internal
systems. It's very common that you see
people with a spreadsheet open where
they're taking notes which is their you
know scratch pad or you know their their
context window for integrating across
multiple different internal systems.
>> Yes., Yeah., Yeah., Absolutely., Absolutely.
We've talked a bit about organizational
change, but I wanted to throw something
else in here, which is that I think that
in leadership positions, you can often
actually affect a huge amount of change
possibly even more change, without
necessarily
messing around with an org chart very
much. It's kind of like the reversal of
that thing of you have to be really
careful what you say as a leader because
what you say is much more important than
what you do, as it were. But I think I
think sometimes we go to the real
because it seems like that's what we
need to do. But I think quite often
there are maybe less high-profile ways
to affect change that are that are
perhaps
more effective or or in some cases
easier to to to do.
>> I, don't, know, if, I, would, say, easier,, but
I would say more effective and less
disruptive. So I agree with you. Reorgs
are disruptive.
Sometimes
in rare circumstances, the disruption is
what you desire out of a reorg, but but
that's, usually, [clears throat], not, what
I'm going for. One of the ways that you
can create change is in what you
celebrate and the the sort of stories
and myths that you tell.
So, you know, if you if you celebrate
